result.summary: The poet praises Aphrodite, who was carried by the west wind over the sea to Cyprus. The Hours dress and adorn her and bring her to the gods, who all wish to marry her. The poet then prays for victory in a song contest.

scenes.title: Aphrodite's birth and adornment
scenes.summary: Aphrodite is borne by the wind to Cyprus, where the Hours dress her in gold and present her to the gods, who each wish to wed her.

scenes.title: Prayer for victory
scenes.summary: The poet greets the goddess and asks for victory in the contest, promising to remember her and another song.

characters.name: Aphrodite
characters.description: gold-crowned goddess of beauty who came over the sea to Cyprus

characters.name: Hours
characters.description: gold-filleted attendants who welcome and dress Aphrodite

alias_notes.explanation: Epithet of Aphrodite, linked with the island of Cythera.

notable_quotes.reason: Vivid image of Aphrodite's birth from the sea foam arriving at Cyprus.

analysis.text: The hymn celebrates Aphrodite's beauty and power, shown by how all the gods desire her.
Homeric Hymns were prefaces sung by rhapsodes before longer recitations, as the closing request for victory in a contest suggests.

legacy.text: The image of Aphrodite arriving over the sea inspired later art, such as Botticelli's The Birth of Venus (c. 1485).

fun_facts.text: Orichalc, mentioned in her jewelry, is an ancient metal whose exact identity is still uncertain.

language_notes.text: Wafted means carried gently through the air or over water; the wind moves Aphrodite to shore.
Orichalc is a prized metal of ancient tradition, often described as gleaming like gold; its exact nature is uncertain.
Cytherea is a title of Aphrodite, linked to the island of Cythera, another place of her worship.
"Order you my song" means arrange or direct my song for you, asking her to favour its performance.

context_notes.text: Cyprus was a chief centre of Aphrodite's worship, so the hymn begins by naming her island domain.
The Hours are goddesses of the seasons and natural order, here serving as Aphrodite's attendants.
Hymn singers competed at festivals; the poet asks the goddess for success in such a contest.

literary_notes.text: Compound descriptors like "gold-crowned" and "stately" fix Aphrodite's traditional splendour at the hymn's opening.
A catalogue of gold, crown and snow-white skin builds a dazzling visual picture of her adornment.
The poet turns to address the goddess directly, shifting from narrative to prayer.
